headline: AMZN is up about 12% premarket as AWS growth hit 37%, while AAPL is down about 7% on a supply-capped September forecast.
quick: Apple and Amazon both reported Thursday after the close. Overnight has not changed the verdict: Amazon is bid up, Apple is marked down.
Amazon's headline EPS of $5.75 is not a real number. A $53.4B one-off gain, mostly its Anthropic stake, did most of it. Operating income up 43% is the actual beat.
Chips ripped Thursday on no company news: SOXX +8%, MRVL +13%, INTC +11%. That was Microsoft's spending plus a memory shortage. NBIS rose 27% on a separate story — a forced seller being cleared out.

Timing note. This edition replaces the one written at 20:27 Thursday evening. It fired on time at 07:00 New York, before Friday's open. Thursday's close is settled; the premarket moves below are thin, provisional, and the bell will settle them.

macro.dt: The Fed held at 3.5–3.75% on Wednesday, 9–3, with three members wanting a rise. Futures now put a 54% chance on a hike on 16 September
macro.dd: Note the direction. The market is pricing the next move as up, not down. Higher rates raise borrowing costs and cut what investors will pay per dollar of distant earnings. That hits fast-growing tech hardest, because most of its profit sits far in the future.

macro.dt: June core PCE, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, came in Thursday at 3.3% year-over-year, matching forecasts, with monthly prices up 0.1% against 0.2% expected
macro.dd: The annual rate is uncomfortably high but the monthly number is the softer one, and it is what the Fed watches for turning points. A cooler month takes a little pressure off the rate-hike case above.

macro.dt: Second-quarter GDP grew 1.5%, down from 2.1% and below the ~2% expected
macro.dd: Slower growth reaches consumer spending first. That lands on Apple and on Amazon's retail arm, rather than on cloud, where demand is contracted years ahead.

macro.dt: Samsung warned the memory shortage may run into 2028. A new tariff schedule took effect 24 July after the temporary 10% global tariff lapsed
macro.dd: Both are input costs, not sentiment. Memory now shows up in two places at once: Apple's gross margin and Amazon's building budget. It is the single thread running through both of Thursday's reports.

macro.dt: QQQ rose about 3.4% Thursday; the Nasdaq Composite rose exactly 2.8% to 25,122.18, ending a six-day slide. The S&P 500 closed +1.7% at 7,437.64
macro.dd: This contradicts the weak GDP print and a Fed the market thinks may hike next. Tech ignored the macro entirely and traded on Microsoft's cloud numbers. Read the day as a single-stock event that spread, not as a verdict on the economy.

entries.happened: Amazon reported Q2 on Thursday after the close, and AWS growth accelerated to its fastest in about five years.
figures: Revenue     $200.6B vs $196.4B expected  (+20% y/y)
AWS         $42.2B vs $40.5B expected  +37% vs ~31% expected — fastest in 18 quarters
AWS profit $16.6B vs $10.2B a year ago  (39% margin, up ~6.5 points)
Operating income $27.5B, +43% y/y
EPS $5.75 — includes a $53.4B one-off gain, mostly the Anthropic stake; strip it and it sits near the ~$1.81 expected
Backlog (revenue already under contract) $496B
Advertising $19.8B, +26%
2026 capex guide raised to ~$220B from ~$200B; twelve-month free cash flow swung to -$7.6B from +$18.2B
Q3 revenue guide $197–202B vs $204B expected — a miss
entries.why: AWS growth is the number Amazon's price is set on, and it sped up instead of fading. A $496B backlog turns guesswork about future growth into revenue already signed for, which is why investors tolerate the spending: it is filling orders, not placing a bet. Rising margin alongside rising growth is the rarest combination in large-cap tech, because it says Amazon can fill capacity without spending more per dollar earned. Treat the headline EPS as noise. A paper markup on a stake Amazon has not sold tells you nothing about the business.

foot.v: Largely. Shares rose about 9–10% after hours Thursday and are near +12% in Friday premarket, so the overnight session has extended the move rather than faded it. Still provisional: premarket volume is thin and the open settles it. Note the market bought this despite a revenue guide below expectations.
AWS growth stalls next quarter while capex stays at $220B, turning the spend into a margin problem before the contracted revenue arrives.
Q3 results, late October.

entries.happened: Apple beat on every headline line on Thursday after the close, then guided the September quarter well below the pace it had just set.
figures: Revenue     $109.4B vs $108.65B expected  (+16% y/y)
EPS          $2.02 vs $1.89 expected  (vs $1.57 a year ago), including $0.11 from tariff refunds
Gross margin 50.1% vs 46.5% a year ago — about 2 points of that from tariff refunds
iPhone      $54.25B, +22% — a June-quarter record
Services $30.74B, +12%, vs ~$31.2B expected — and down sequentially for the first time since 2022
Greater China $18.82B, +22%, vs ~$19.6B expected
September-quarter guide +9–11% y/y vs ~12% expected, down from +16%; gross margin guided to 47–48%
Dividend $0.27, payable 13 August
entries.why: Apple is short of parts, not demand. Cook said iPhone and Mac orders ran ahead of forecast. But a supply ceiling caps revenue in the quarter that carries the holiday, and that is the quarter the year is judged on. Cook called memory pricing a "100-year flood": each device costs more to build while the retail price stays fixed, so the extra cost lands entirely on the 50.1% gross margin that funds the buyback. Services slipping sequentially matters more than the iPhone beat, because Services is the high-margin, recurring line that earns Apple its premium multiple in the first place.

foot.v: Yes, and the overnight session confirmed it. Shares fell 6.65% to $311.25 after hours from a $333.43 close, and sit near -7% in Friday premarket. Sources differ slightly on the after-hours print: some report -6.3% to $312.33. That fall is the guidance, not the quarter: shares rose with the market during Thursday's session, before the release landed.
Memory contract prices ease, or Apple signals it will pass the cost through on the autumn iPhone.
September-quarter results, late October; iPhone launch event expected September. This was Tim Cook's last earnings call as CEO.

note_after.title: The asymmetry — same night, same excuse, opposite reactions
note_after.body: Amazon guided revenue below expectations and rose. Apple beat and guided to 9–11% growth, and fell. Both blamed the same memory shortage. The difference is what the extra cost buys. Amazon's higher spending buys revenue-generating capacity against a $496B booked backlog, so its shortfall reads as revenue deferred. Apple's higher cost buys nothing. It just compresses margin on a product whose price is already set, so its shortfall reads as revenue lost. That distinction, not the size of either beat, is what set the two reactions.

entries.happened: Wednesday night's Azure numbers held all the way to Thursday's bell, producing the largest one-day value gain by any stock ever.
figures: Closed +16%, adding roughly $450B — a record
Azure +43%, up from 40% last quarter, and guided to 45% next quarter
Azure passed $100B of annual revenue for the first time
Revenue $90B, +18%; adjusted EPS $4.74 vs $4.24 expected
Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats
entries.why: Azure's growth rate is the single number investors use to price Microsoft. Accelerating rather than decaying extends how many years of that growth they will assume, which lifts the multiple (what they pay per dollar of earnings) more than the profit beat itself. It also answers the year's central worry, that AI spending was going out with no revenue coming back. The second-order effect drives half this list: Microsoft's building programme is revenue for the companies it buys from, which is most of why chips and neoclouds rallied Thursday.

foot.v: Fully. A 16% close is a complete repricing, and it is now settled rather than provisional.
Next quarter's 45% Azure guide is missed, reframing this as a one-quarter capacity catch-up.
FQ1 results, late October.

entries.happened: Meta fell about 9% on Wednesday night's results, which sit just outside this window.
figures: Revenue $60.8B, +28% y/y
EPS $6.18, missing by about 14% on legal and severance charges
Free cash flow collapsed to $784M from ~$8.6B a year earlier; quarterly capex $31.1B
Full-year capex guide raised to $130–145B
Q3 revenue guide $61–64B vs $63.15B expected
entries.why: This is the asymmetry of the week. Microsoft and Meta both raised AI spending enormously, and the market treated them oppositely. Microsoft could point at Azure accelerating, so the spending reads as capacity it can already sell. Meta's own revenue line is not accelerating, so the same spending reads as cost with no visible customer. Near-zero free cash flow also removes the buyback that has underpinned the shares. That test is what investors then applied to Amazon on Thursday night, and Amazon passed it.

foot.v: Yes, and it happened before this window opened. The move followed the news, so it is a genuine reaction — but it is not today's news.
Meta puts a revenue number on its AI spending, or trims the capex range.
Q3 results, late October.

entries.happened: Nebius posted its biggest one-day gain of 2026 on no company news in the window.
figures: Closed +26.7% — largest single-day gain of 2026
Still well down on the month
Citadel bought most of hedge fund Situational Awareness's roughly $16B public book after margin calls
The $1B+ Reflection AI contract several outlets recycled on Thursday was announced 14 July
entries.why: This is flows, not fundamentals. A leveraged fund was forced to liquidate its whole book on margin calls, and Citadel took the other side. A forced seller pushes a price below what the business is worth, because the selling answers a margin call rather than a view on value; clearing that seller lets the price snap back. Amazon's $220B capex guide added fuel, but nothing about Nebius's contracts, costs or customers changed on Thursday.

foot.v: There was no company news to price. A 27% move driven by a forced seller clearing is a change in who owns the shares, not in what they are worth.
A hyperscaler signals it will build in-house rather than rent third-party capacity.
Q2 results, expected late August.

entries.happened: Marvell rose 13% with the semiconductor group. No company announcement in the window.
figures: SOXX chip index +8% on the day
SOXX had fallen 27.4% in July — its worst month since September 2001
Marvell had fallen 7% as recently as 28 July
Company news was small: a $250M India investment announced 29 July, and a routine $0.06 dividend paid Thursday
entries.why: Two things drove this and neither came from Marvell. Microsoft's cloud growth told the market that AI orders are real, and Samsung's warning that the memory shortage runs into 2028 told it that supply is tight. Custom-silicon names are geared to hyperscaler budgets, so they move hardest when those budgets are confirmed — and Amazon then confirmed $220B after the bell. After a 27% drawdown, a rebound of this size is as much positioning unwinding as new information.

foot.v: No company news existed to price. Do not read a 13% day as a Marvell event.
A hyperscaler shifts custom-silicon orders to a rival.
Q2 results, expected late August or early September — sources differ.

note_after.title: Beware one figure circulating this morning
note_after.body: Some coverage this morning claims Marvell fell 14% on results, citing adjusted EPS of $0.67 on revenue of $2.01B. Marvell has not reported. Its next release is not due until late August at the earliest. That item is recycled from a report a year old. Fresh coverage of an old event is still an old event — and in this case, the wrong company's quarter entirely.

entries.happened: Intel rose 11% to $91.13 with the chip group. No company announcement in the window.
figures: Closed +11% at $91.13, after falling 6% on 28 July
Moved with SOXX +8%
Intel last reported on 23 July — a week ago, not Thursday
entries.why: The memory-shortage story is the cleanest read-through here. When capacity is scarce across the industry, buyers widen their supplier list, and Intel is the obvious second source. That improves the odds its foundry business fills capacity, which is the swing factor for margins. Nothing was confirmed on Thursday, so this is the market pricing a possibility, not a contract.

foot.v: No company news to price. Sector move. The 23 July quarter (revenue $16.1B, +25%, and non-GAAP EPS of $0.42 against $0.21 expected) was priced a week ago.
The memory squeeze eases and second-source urgency fades.
Q3 results, expected late October.

entries.happened: Tesla closed at $308.82, up 3.5%, on no company news.
figures: Follows six straight down days totalling -21%
That slide erased roughly $261B of market value
Last reported 22 July
entries.why: This is a rebound inside a broad market rally, not a change in the Tesla story. The useful number is the one before it: a 21% fall over six sessions is a large de-rating, and a single 3.5% day recovers little of it. Nothing in the last 24 hours addressed why the stock fell in the first place.

foot.v: Nothing to price. The move tracked the index.
Q3 deliveries, early October.

entries.happened: Nvidia rose with the chip group to about $195. No company announcement.
figures: Closed up about 2.9%, near $195
Lagged MRVL (+13%) and INTC (+11%) badly
entries.why: The lag is the interesting part. On 28 July the market narrowed the AI chip trade towards Nvidia while peers sold off; on Thursday that reversed, and money went to the names that had been discarded. That is a rotation within the sector, not a judgement on Nvidia. The genuine read-through is positive and arrived after the bell: Amazon at $220B and Meta at $130–145B of 2026 capex are Nvidia's order book.

foot.v: No company news to price. Amazon's raised capex guide landed after Nvidia's close, so Friday's session is the first chance to price it.
Q2 results, expected late August.

entries.happened: Robinhood beat clearly on Wednesday after the close, and drifted up on Thursday.
figures: Revenue $1.308B, +32% y/y — a record
Net income $561M, +45%
EPS $0.62 vs ~$0.41 expected
Crypto revenue -38% y/y to $100M
Event contracts $156M — now bigger than equities at $129M
Fell 3.15% to $89.84 on Wednesday — before the results landed
entries.why: The mix, not the total, is what to watch. Growth came from event contracts, a young line with unproven durability and unsettled regulation, while crypto — the high-margin engine that carried prior quarters — nearly halved. Investors pay less per dollar of earnings when they cannot tell whether those earnings recur. A large beat that produced only a drift upwards says the market is discounting the quality of it, not its size.

foot.v: Partly. Note the sequence: the 3.15% fall to $89.84 happened in Wednesday's session, before the release. It was not a reaction to this quarter.
Event-contract revenue holds up for another two quarters and crypto stabilises.
4 November.

readthrough.title: One shortage, showing up in three places
readthrough.body: The memory squeeze is the thread tying the week together. Samsung says it may run to 2028. Apple felt it as cost: Cook's "100-year flood" forced price rises and now presses on a 50.1% gross margin, with September margin guided down to 47–48%. Amazon felt it as capital — part of why the 2026 capex guide went to $220B from $200B. The chipmakers felt it as pricing power, which is why MRVL, INTC and the memory names rallied hardest. The same fact is a cost to whoever buys parts and revenue to whoever sells them. Separately, the hyperscaler budgets now on the table (Amazon at $220B, Meta at $130–145B) are a direct read-through to NVDA, MRVL and NBIS. A cloud company's building programme is its suppliers' order book.

note.title: What is not today's news
note.body: Alphabet reported on 22 July; its capex rise to as much as $205B is nine days old. Palantir closed at $122.05, reports Monday, and had nothing in the window. Nebius's $1B+ Reflection AI contract, republished by several outlets on Thursday, was signed on 14 July and did not cause the 27% move. Intel's blowout quarter was 23 July, not Thursday. And Marvell has not reported at all, whatever this morning's coverage says.
